title: Given a sorted array (or a sorted linked list), remove the duplicate elements in place so that each element appears only once, and return the new length (or the de-duplicated list). Solve it without allocating a second structure. (LeetCode: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List / Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array)
shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Structure (Two Pointers, In Place)

s1_definition.profdef: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses a slow-fast two-pointer scheme. The slow pointer marks the end of the unique prefix built so far, and the fast pointer scans ahead. Whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the last unique value, you copy it to the position just after the slow pointer and advance the slow pointer. The unique count is the slow pointer plus one. For a sorted linked list, you walk a single pointer and skip over nodes whose value equals the current node.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a sorted ledger of account numbers where the same account can appear several times in a row because of repeated entries. He wants a clean ledger with each account listed once. He keeps one finger on the last unique account he has confirmed and reads forward; whenever he sees an account different from that last unique one, he writes it right after his confirmed section and moves his confirming finger forward. Because the ledger is sorted, all copies of the same account sit together, so this one sweep is enough.
s1_definition.oneliner: In sorted data, duplicates are neighbors, so one slow-fast sweep keeps only the first of each run.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses a slow-fast two-pointer scheme. The slow pointer marks the end of the unique prefix built so far, and the fast pointer scans ahead. Whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the last unique value, you copy it to the position just after the slow pointer and advance the slow pointer. The unique count is the slow pointer plus one. For a sorted linked list, you walk a single pointer and skip over nodes whose value equals the current node.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a sorted ledger of account numbers where the same account can appear several times in a row because of repeated entries. He wants a clean ledger with each account listed once. He keeps one finger on the last unique account he has confirmed and reads forward; whenever he sees an account different from that last unique one, he writes it right after his confirmed section and moves his confirming finger forward. Because the ledger is sorted, all copies of the same account sit together, so this one sweep is enough.

**One line to remember:** In sorted data, duplicates are neighbors, so one slow-fast sweep keeps only the first of each run.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the input is sorted, every group of equal values is contiguous. That is the key fact: to remove duplicates we only ever need to compare each element to the previous kept element, never to all earlier elements.

For the array version, we keep a `slow` index pointing at the last unique element, starting at 0. We scan with a `fast` index from 1 to the end. If `arr[fast]` differs from `arr[slow]`, we increment `slow` and copy `arr[fast]` into `arr[slow]`. If they are equal, we skip. After the scan, positions 0 through `slow` hold the unique values, and the unique count is `slow + 1`. The elements beyond that are leftover and ignored.

A finance usage example: suppose a sorted account-number array is `[101, 101, 102, 103, 103, 103, 104]`. We start with `slow=0` (value 101). At `fast=1` the value 101 equals `arr[slow]`, skip. At `fast=2` the value 102 differs, so `slow` becomes 1 and we copy 102 there. At `fast=3` the value 103 differs, so `slow` becomes 2 and we copy 103. The repeated 103s are skipped, and finally 104 is copied. The unique prefix becomes `[101, 102, 103, 104]` with a count of 4.

For the sorted linked list version, we walk a `current` pointer. While `current` and `current.next` both exist and have equal values, we bypass the duplicate by setting `current.next = current.next.next`, which unlinks the duplicate node. Otherwise we advance `current`. This removes all consecutive duplicates in one pass with constant extra space.

The senior-level nuance: the array method does not shrink the physical array because Java arrays have fixed length, so we return the logical length and treat the tail as garbage. A common variant allows each element to appear at most twice, which you handle by comparing `arr[fast]` against `arr[slow - 1]` instead of `arr[slow]`. For the linked list, using a dummy head is unnecessary for this basic version because the head itself is always kept, but a dummy becomes useful in the harder variant that removes all nodes that ever had a duplicate.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India imports a sorted feed of account numbers from a partner system, but the feed often contains the same account repeated several times in a row because of overlapping export windows. Before the reconciliation engine runs, we must collapse those repeats so each account appears exactly once, otherwise the engine double-counts balances. Because the feed can be huge, we cannot afford to allocate a second array.

Problem 2 — The same cleanup is sometimes needed on a sorted linked list of transaction references streamed in order, where consecutive identical references must be merged into one. We want a single clean pass with no extra structure.

The code defines a `LedgerDeduplicator` class with two methods: `removeDuplicates` for a sorted int array returning the unique count, and `removeDuplicates` overloaded for a sorted linked list of account references returning the cleaned head. A runnable demo seeds both a sorted array and a sorted linked list, cleans them, and logs the results.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sorted array `[101, 101, 102, 103, 103, 103, 104]` and the sorted list `501 -> 501 -> 502 -> 503 -> 503`.

Step 1: For the array, `slow` starts at 0 pointing at 101. The fast scan begins at index 1.

Step 2: At `fast=1` the value 101 equals `arr[slow]`, so it is a duplicate and skipped.

Step 3: At `fast=2` the value 102 differs, so `slow` becomes 1 and 102 is copied there. The front is now `[101, 102, ...]`.

Step 4: At `fast=3` the value 103 differs, so `slow` becomes 2 and 103 is copied. The two further 103s at `fast=4` and `fast=5` are equal and skipped.

Step 5: At `fast=6` the value 104 differs, so `slow` becomes 3 and 104 is copied. The scan ends with `slow=3`, so the unique count is 4 and the front holds `[101, 102, 103, 104]`.

Step 6: For the linked list, `current` starts at node 501. Its next is also 501, so that next node is unlinked. Now 501 points to 502, which differs, so `current` advances. 502 points to 503, differs, advance. 503 points to another 503, which is unlinked. The list is now `501 -> 502 -> 503`.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 5:55:00 PM com.bank.ledger.DedupDemo main
INFO: Array unique count = 4
INFO: Unique accounts: [101, 102, 103, 104]
INFO: Linked list duplicates removed.
INFO: Unique refs: [501, 502, 503]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted structure in place relies on one key fact: because the data is sorted, every group of equal values sits together, so I only ever need to compare each element to the previous kept element rather than to everything before it. That lets me solve it in a single linear pass with constant extra space using a slow-fast two-pointer scheme.

For the array version I keep a slow pointer at the last unique element and scan forward with a fast pointer. Whenever the fast element differs from the slow element, I advance the slow pointer and copy the fast element into that position, building the unique prefix in place. When the scan finishes, the slow pointer plus one is the count of unique elements, and everything beyond that is leftover garbage that I simply ignore, because Java arrays cannot physically shrink. For the sorted linked list version I walk a single pointer and, whenever the next node has the same value as the current node, I unlink it by pointing current's next past the duplicate, which removes all consecutive duplicates in one sweep.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this solved a real reconciliation problem. We imported a sorted feed of account numbers from a partner, but overlapping export windows produced the same account repeated several times in a row, and feeding those repeats into the reconciliation engine would double-count balances. The feed was large, so allocating a second array was not acceptable, and the in-place slow-fast sweep collapsed the repeats cheaply before reconciliation ran. We used the same idea on a sorted linked list of transaction references that streamed in order.

The senior-level point I add is about the common variants. If the requirement allows each element to appear at most twice, I compare the fast element against the element two positions back instead of one, which keeps exactly two copies. And for the harder linked-list variant that removes every node that ever had a duplicate, I introduce a dummy head node so I have a stable handle on the node before a run of duplicates, since in that case even the original head might be removed. Knowing which variant the interviewer means, and adjusting the comparison accordingly, is what shows real command of the pattern.
